text:
1. Johnson does not base his judgment of the work on his own admiration.
2. One person's admiration might reflect only the tastes of one age and one temperament.
3. Johnson judges a work by asking what time has done to it.
4. A writer whose fame depends on the fashion of his day, local customs, or party quarrels may be praised while that fashion lasts.
5. Fashions pass, and praise that depends on them passes too.
6. Only works that keep pleasing readers who share none of the circumstances of their original audience can be said to have proved their worth.
7. Later readers who share none of the original audience's circumstances bring no partiality to judging a work.
8. Such later readers have no friendship with the author.
9. Such later readers have no stake in the author's opinions.
10. Such later readers read the author only because his work still gives pleasure.
